study_period.note: The article distinguishes the emergency-period admission cohorts from the later survey windows; do not conflate these dates.

sources.design: Questionnaire survey and telephone semi-structured interviews
sources.population: Patients admitted to Tokyo Medical and Dental University Hospital for COVID-19 moderate II or severe respiratory failure during selected emergency-declaration periods and family members who received treatment explanations

interviews.family_relationships: Two spouses/partners and two children among four family interviewees

sources.abstract_findings: Approximately 90% of patients and family members reported understanding treatment explanations; 51.1% of patients (23/45) reported not expressing or being unable to express treatment preferences, or not remembering/knowing; ACP awareness was low.
sources.source_sha256_note: Publisher PDF inspected via web viewer; not stored in GitHub and no hash is claimed.
limitations: Single hospital (Tokyo Medical and Dental University Hospital)
Only patients discharged alive after moderate II or severe respiratory failure were included; not all COVID-19 patients or those who died
Patients who were unable to participate and those with altered consciousness at admission are not directly represented by patient questionnaire responses
Survey recall could be up to 13 months after hospitalization; authors explicitly note recall uncertainty
Questionnaire denominators vary by item (e.g. n=43/44 for understanding, n=45/44 for preference); do not use total respondent count as denominator for every item
Combined 51.1% patient category includes no expression, inability to express, and not remembering/knowing; it is not a direct measure of incapacity or refusal
Interview sample is only 6 patients and 4 family members; qualitative findings are not prevalence estimates
Single-center results cannot establish national prevalence or causal effects of visitation restrictions

sampling.selection: Only patients discharged alive after admission for moderate II or severe respiratory failure in the specified emergency-period cohorts; family members who received treatment explanations.

full_text_extraction.pages: PDF pp.22-31 (methods, results, discussion and conclusion)

decision_expression.patients: 23/45 (51.1%) combined category: did not express/could not express/did not remember or know; categories must not be conflated with refusal or incapacity

authors_suggested_measures: Make multiple family members available to participate in surrogate decision-making while clarifying a key contact person
Provide families with regular updates on patient condition
Provide accurate public information about invasive treatments and standard treatment pathways
Promote ACP through hospital posters and leaflets and public online programs

crosschecked_sections: PDF pp.22-31: methods, respondent counts, consciousness/explanation status, explanation understanding, treatment preference, ACP knowledge, interviews, discussion and conclusions

interview subgroup 6 patients and 4 families; 4/6 patient no consciousness; 2/4 family surrogate burden; 5/6 patient acceptance of family decision

main_findings: 6/8 (75%) patient/family respondents accepted visitation restrictions; 1/8 expressed infection concern; 1/8 sadness about inability to visit even when condition worsened
5/8 (62.5%) considered telephone explanation acceptable; some could not imagine patient condition without images/visual information
Communication methods: telephone 6/10 (60%), remote visit 3/10 (30%), Zoom 1/10 (10%), LINE 1/10 (10%); multiple responses
Desired remote-visit frequency: daily 6/10 (60%), weekly 2/10 (20%), 2-3 times weekly 2/10 (20%)
Preferred remote-visit method: hospital iPad 4/10 (40%), family at home using device 6/10 (60%)
Healthcare workers: telephone 11/11 (100%), face-to-face outpatient explanation 6/11 (55%), remote visit 2/11 (18%); methods not mutually exclusive
9/11 (81%) healthcare workers said explanation or policy decisions became more difficult; 2/11 (18%) reported no change

Qualitative findings: difficulty imagining ADL/home situation without visual contact; after-hours workload; end-of-life guilt; difficulty supporting family understanding; remote visits difficult for older adults with hearing loss and time-consuming for staff
extraction.methodology: Semi-structured interviews of approximately 15 minutes; audio recording not used; interviewer notes transcribed after interviews; co-researchers discussed analytical reliability and validity.
limitations: Single-center
Retrospective recall bias
Purposive selection/selection bias
Potential physician-interviewer/doctor-patient relationship bias
Small qualitative sample; not prevalence evidence
One subgroup's exact composition is not fully specified in extracted results; respondent labels preserve article wording
